fields.title: Measuring a change, not just looking at a chart
fields.keyTakeaway: What counts as success is decided before release, not after. A pre-defined number tests a hypothesis; the exact same number found on a chart afterward merely confirms what you already believed.
fields.checkQuestion: After a release, the metric grew by 4%. What is missing to attribute this growth to the release?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **how much did changes impact value?** In the HEART lesson, we selected what to monitor continuously. Here it is different: verifying a specific change.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you don't answer this question.** After a release, people open a dashboard, find a metric that went up, and declare success. A metric that dropped fails to make it into the report—not out of malice, but because people were looking for confirmation.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Four lines, each guarding against a specific mistake
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **By how much**—the exact number that will count as success. "Will grow" is not enough.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Over what timeframe**—an observation window chosen based on scenario frequency, not impatience.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **What must not deteriorate**—a guardrail metric. This is what catches cases where you win in one area and lose in another.
fields.blocks/3/text: The fourth item is skipped most often, yet it is the most valuable. Almost any change improves something; the question is always at what expense.
fields.blocks/4/text:
Recorded before release: store inventory time will drop from 90 to 70 minutes over three weeks; discrepancy rate after audit will not increase.

Three weeks later: 68 minutes—success on the primary metric. But the discrepancy rate grew from 3% to 7%: people started scanning faster and missed barcodes more often, while the app silently accepted it.

Without a guardrail metric, the release would have been logged as a win. With it, it became clear that a follow-up task was needed—confirmation on a suspicious jump in stock count.
fields.blocks/5/text: A before/after measurement does not prove causality: seasonality, marketing, or another release could have happened in between. Causality requires a control group—a holdout or at least a segment that didn't receive the change. More on this in the experiment module.
